P01.author: E
P01.explanation: Rinsing dyed wool in the current left the water below the mill stained and empty of trout and insect larvae, while trout thrived above it, so the mill fouled the stream: it "soured" it. "Siphoned" means drew water away, but the whole stream ran past the wheel. "Stilled" means calmed the current, but the wheel turned in the open current with no pond to slow it. "Walled" means hemmed in with walls, but the dye marked gravel bars and alder roots along both banks, which are natural banks, not walls.

P02.author: C
P02.explanation: "Depository" fits: while the museum had no building, its paintings were packed, locked away in the mine's steady air, and returned untouched, so the mine kept them safe until they were needed again. "Gallery" fails because the crates stayed sealed and no one was let in, so nothing was shown to anyone. "Hospital" fails because the canvases came back exactly as they were packed; the mine's air protected them, but no painting was treated or mended there. "Dump" fails because every crate went back up to the new building, so nothing was discarded.

P03.author: E
P03.explanation: The monastery earned more from wine and beer sold to travelers on the road than from its fields and let its beds by the night, so it served the valley as a place where passers-by paid to drink and eat: a "tavern." A "sanatorium" takes in the sick, but in plague years the monastery shut its gate and served only through a hatch. A "scriptorium" is where books are copied, but its dozen books were all bought in the city. A "vault" keeps valuables safe, but it kept no money overnight and sent each week's takings to the bishop.

P04.author: D
P04.explanation: The translator moved the story to an English village, turned its fjord into an estuary and its money into shillings, and gave every character an English name, so he "naturalized" the novel, making it at home in English life. "Lightened" fails because every drowning and every winter of hunger is told in full, so the book is as grim as before. "Mutilated" fails because he kept every chapter, cutting nothing. "Manicured" fails because his sentences keep the original's short, abrupt rhythm clause by clause, so he did not smooth the author's style.

P05.author: D
P05.explanation: The receding water left a layer of bark, leaves and straw, and under it the corn stayed green through a drought and the usual early-summer weeds barely appeared, so the flood had "mulched" the field: covered it in a layer that held moisture and kept weeds down. "Manured" fails because the soil's nitrogen was the same as before the flood, so the debris kept the corn green by holding water in, not by feeding it. "Leached" fails because that same unchanged nitrogen in the top foot shows nothing was washed down out of the topsoil. "Mired" fails because, damp as the soil under the layer was, the corn went into it on schedule, so the field was never too wet to work.

P06.author: A
P06.explanation: "Cafeteria" fits: forest voles come into the strip at night, where stems are clipped of their seed heads, and are home again by morning, so they use it as a place to feed. "Corridor" fails because no vole goes more than a few hundred yards from its own forest, so none travels along the strip to the other one. "Cage" fails because the voles return to the forest every morning and nest there, so the strip does not hold them. "Cemetery" fails because voles that visit the strip outlive those that stay in the forest.

P07.author: D
P07.explanation: Most visitors came by train or car from beyond the district and stayed three hours, and restaurants opened along the streets facing the park, so it is the district's "magnet," drawing people in from elsewhere. "Junction" fails because a junction is a place people pass through on the way somewhere else, and these visitors made the park their destination and stayed for hours. "Mixer" fails because residents of the two neighborhoods the yard once divided were only a tenth of the crowd, so the park was not chiefly where those two communities came together. "Muffler" fails because the park's lawns and concert shell lie open to the highway, with nothing between the traffic and the homes to absorb its noise.

P08.author: E
P08.explanation: Every stone was rounded, and the floods that roll them fill the water with fine grit, so the river had worn the stones down by grinding them with grit: it had "sanded" them. "Sorted" means separated by size, but the sieved mix of sizes was the same at the cliffs as at the sea. "Stacked" means set one on another, but painted stones moved a mile downstream with each flood and lay wherever they stopped. "Stained" means given a color from outside, but a cracked stone showed the same shade inside as out.

P09.author: B
P09.explanation: The asphalt softened each summer and the trucks, always in the same wheel tracks, pressed it down a little more each year, most where they crawled up the climb, so the surface had been "rutted": worn into grooves along the wheel paths. "Rippled" fails because the trucks pressed the asphalt down along their tracks, and where they braked hard at the stop sign, the place that would shove asphalt into folds, it never shifted. "Raised" fails because the stakes showed the roadbed still at its laid height. "Ruptured" fails because the asphalt never cracked; it sank where the wheels ran.

P10.author: A
P10.explanation: "Chilled" fits: the turbines release water from the bottom of a deep reservoir, and below the dam trout have replaced bass, which now live only thirty miles downstream, so the river below has turned cold. "Bled" fails because the gravel bars lie as deep under water as before 1960, so the river below carries as much water as ever; the bass left for another reason. "Churned" fails because the release is even day and night, and the May flood over the spillway is the river's own snowmelt flood, which came before the dam too. "Clogged" fails because that flood still rolls the gravel bars every year, so silt and plants cannot settle and choke the channel.

P11.author: C
P11.explanation: "Furrowed" fits: the sheep walk the same level tracks, one below another, until hooves have worn them down to earth, so the flock has cut lines into the hillside. "Denuded" fails because the grass between the tracks grows as fully as on the ungrazed slope; only the narrow tracks are bare. "Groomed" fails because that grass is as rough and tall as on the other side, not cropped neat. "Fertilized" fails because the slope's soil tests no richer than the ungrazed slope's.

P12.author: D
P12.explanation: In near-freezing water too poor in oxygen for worms, the hull stood with its masts, painted carvings, coiled ropes and wine intact, its oak still hard, so the sea had "mummified" the ship, preserving it whole. "Interred" fails because the hull stood upright on the open bottom with its masts standing, so it was not buried. "Jostled" fails because it stood where it settled, ropes still coiled on deck. "Mined" fails because the boring worms that tunnel through ship timbers cannot live in that cold, oxygen-poor water, and the oak came up hard enough to take a nail.

P13.author: C
P13.explanation: "Fortified" fits: behind the ivy the mortar had turned to sand, so the stones there were held only by the woody stems woven through them, and that half stood through a gale that brought down the bare half, so the ivy strengthened the wall. "Dislodged" fails because, although stems run among loose stones, no stone on the ivy half fell; it was the bare half that came down. "Dried" fails because moisture readings behind the leaves matched those on the bare half. "Etched" fails because the stone faces under the stems were clean.

P14.author: C
P14.explanation: "Gnawed" fits: the hull lies exposed in warm water full of shipworms, and a plank that looks smooth outside weighs almost nothing and falls apart, so the wood has been eaten away from within. "Entombed" fails because the current keeps the sand swept off the hull, which lies open on the bottom. "Encrusted" fails because the raised plank was smooth and pale on its surface, with no crust on it. "Dismantled" fails because the hull's outline is still unbroken where it settled; the damage is inside the wood, not a ship taken apart.

P15.author: E
P15.explanation: The sealed holds kept salvors away from sixty chests of silver for seventy-four years, and every chest was found where the manifest placed it, so the hull kept a valuable cargo secure: a "strongbox." A "tomb" holds the dead, but the crew were taken off by a schooner the next morning. A "trellis" is a framework things grow along, but its plates lie furred with silt in murky water. A "tripwire" is a hidden hazard that catches the unwary, but it lies far below the keels of passing ships.

P16.author: A
P16.explanation: "Ballroom" fits: groupers gather by the thousand for a few nights after one full moon, the males darken and circle the females, and the females leave a fifth lighter, having shed their eggs, so the outcrop is where the groupers court and spawn. "Canteen" fails because the females lose a fifth of their weight while there, even with swarms of small fish around them, so the groupers are not feeding. "Bedroom" fails because the fish are active at dusk, circling, and leave within a week. "Clinic" fails because a crowd of thousands timed to one full moon a year, with males circling females, is a mating gathering, not fish coming one by one to have parasites removed.

P17.author: C
P17.explanation: "Gilded" fits: the coast is copied exactly at the same size and orientation, and everything new on the print is ornament, whales and a galleon in empty water and a gold-leafed frame for the title, so the engraver dressed up the survey without changing it. "Doctored" fails because every cape, bay, and shoal sits where the survey puts it; the additions are pictures in open water, not false facts about the coast. "Flipped" fails because north is at the top of both. "Enlarged" fails because the print is the survey's size.

P18.author: A
P18.explanation: "Ambushed" fits: the wolves lay hidden in the thickets beside crossings the elk visited every evening, and the elk fell within a few yards of that cover. "Chased" fails because elk struck there went down within three strides, so the kills involved no pursuit. "Corralled" fails because the wolves waited where the elk came on their own each evening; nothing drove the herd into that place. "Cowed" fails because the herd kept using the same crossings and kept the willows browsed to knee height, so the danger did not change where the elk went.

P19.author: E
P19.explanation: Each dry summer browned every pine's needles and stripped them early, while the trees regrew them each spring and grew normally once the rain returned, so the damage was a browning of the foliage that left the trees sound: the drought "scorched" the forest. "Sapped" means drained of strength, but growth rings returned to their old width and beetles that seek weakened pines found few hosts. "Winnowed" means removed the weak and left the strong, but only a few pines died, large and small alike. "Toppled" means knocked over, but the pines that died stayed standing until they rotted.

P20.author: E
P20.explanation: Every entry survives, but the book is a third shorter because the repetitive tallies and wind notes were cut, so the daughter made the diary more concise without losing its substance: she "tightened" it. "Tidied" means cleaned up the writing, but misspellings like "chickins" were printed as the mother wrote them. "Softened" means toned down, but the curses written after quarrels are printed whole. "Spliced" means joined in material from elsewhere, but nothing in the book comes from outside the notebooks.

P21.author: C
P21.explanation: "Flooded" fits: the dams have turned the creek into ponds that stand four feet deep over the old meadow and have drowned the pines there, so the beavers have put their valley under water. "Dredged" fails because silt settling in the still ponds raises their floors every year; the beavers have filled the creek bed in, not scooped it out. "Deforested" fails because the willows they cut grow back and the slopes keep as many aspens as the next valley; the dead pines were killed by water, not cleared. "Greened" fails because in dry summers the valley turns just as brown as the one without beavers.

P22.author: C
P22.explanation: "Firebreak" fits: the wall stands between the thatched cottages and the trees, and when the whole village burned, the orchard behind it lost only some scorched leaves, so the wall stopped the fire from spreading. "Hearth" fails because frost blackens the blossom on the trees beside the wall as much as on any other, so the wall gives no warmth. "Fence" fails because the wall is open at both ends and runs along one edge only, so it encloses nothing. "Dike" fails because the river lies a mile to the south, on the far side of the orchard from the wall.

P23.author: B
P23.explanation: Seeds under banded shrubs lay where they fell until mice ate them, seeds under ant shrubs vanished within a day, and the island's young shrubs grew on ant nest mounds far from any parent, so the ants "propagated" the shrub by carrying its seeds to new ground. "Pollinated" fails because banded shrubs flowered and podded as well without ants. "Patrolled" fails because caterpillars chewed shrubs with and without ants alike. "Parasitized" fails because the shrubs grew as well either way, and only with ants did their seeds escape the mice and found new plants.

P24.author: A
P24.explanation: "Banquet" fits: hundreds of scavengers crowded onto the carcass at once and ate it all within months, a single huge feast that ended when the flesh was gone. "Cupboard" fails because nothing was kept back to draw on later; a crowd consumed all of it in four months. "Battery" fails because the bones were finished within a year, so the carcass released its energy in a burst rather than slowly over a long time. "Bridge" fails because the scavengers are animals found across the whole seafloor, so the carcass linked no separated populations.

P25.author: D
P25.explanation: Water came in brown with mud and left clear while the marsh floor rose a quarter inch a year, so the marsh catches the mud the water carries and holds it: it is the bay's "net." "Kidney" fails because even read loosely as a filter, a kidney removes the harmful dissolved load from what passes through it, and this water carried all of the creek's fertilizer nitrate on to feed the bay's algae blooms, so the marsh strained out mud while the farms' waste went through untouched. "Lung" fails because the marsh's outflow runs short of oxygen at the same time the bay does, so the marsh cannot be what resupplies the bay with it. "Kitchen" fails because the shrimp near the outlet were living on plankton, so the bay was not being fed from the marsh.

P26.author: B
P26.explanation: At six stops villagers in borrowed armor and painted masks acted out scenes from the village's history while paying visitors followed to watch, so the walk was a "pageant": a series of scenes performed for spectators. "Roundup" fails because the ponies were scattered by the carriages, not gathered. "Pilgrimage" fails because the stops were stages for scenes watched by paying townspeople, not holy places. "Raid" fails because the attack from the neighboring parish was a scene acted at the boundary stone about 1460, not a real foray.

P27.author: B
P27.explanation: Every city paper answered the collection by reprinting its weakest stanza beside a cartoon of a weeping cow, letting the verse mock itself, and the printer sold only forty copies, so her poems had been "panned": held up to ridicule by the critics. "Pirated" fails because the stanzas appeared only as quotations inside reviews, and her printer held the only plates, so no one else printed copies of the book to sell. "Plagiarized" fails because every review printed her name over the stanza it quoted. "Popularized" fails because the reviews drove no sales: forty copies sold and the rest went for scrap.

P28.author: D
P28.explanation: A war tax tripled the price of a paper, circulation halved, two dailies closed and the survivors lost half their reporters, so the government "impoverished" the press, draining its money and its staff. "Muzzled" fails because the survivors printed whatever they pleased, including weekly attacks on the tax and the war, so the press lost money, not its voice. "Mobilized" fails because papers attacking the war every week were not enlisted in it. "Nationalized" fails because both survivors stayed in private hands.

P29.author: B
P29.explanation: The tablet gives the same nine men a monthly barley allowance, cut by a fixed share for the two boys, under the temple overseer's seal, and eleven matching tablets cover the year's other months, so it is the temple's "payroll": its record of wages paid out. "Receipt" fails because the seal is the payer's, the overseer who issued the barley, not that of anyone acknowledging that he had received it, and the tablet stayed in the payer's own storeroom. "Recipe" fails because the lines pair amounts with men's names, not ingredients. "Roadmap" fails because the same nine names recur month after month in one storeroom, so the lines are people, not places on a route.

P30.author: C
P30.explanation: "Drugged" fits: something the workers leave on a leaf slowed aphids to a third of their speed and held back the wings they use to leave, and with that the tended aphids stayed in place while untended ones scattered, so the ants were restraining the aphids chemically. "Herded" fails because the ants never moved the aphids, not even off wilting shoots; the aphids stayed where they settled because they crept slowly after ant contact, which is not driving or steering them anywhere. "Devoured" fails because the clusters on the ants' row grew all summer; that row ended with fewer aphids than the untended one because its slowed, wingless aphids never spread to new plants, not because any were eaten. "Garnered" fails because the aphids stayed out on the stems until the frost killed them; the ants never gathered them in.

P31.author: D
P31.explanation: As the ice melted it left boulders of a rock foreign to the valley scattered across the meadows, so the glacier "littered" the valley floor with them. "Mantled" fails because each boulder rests on the meadows' old soil, which still holds pollen older than the ice, so the glacier spread no layer over the floor; it dropped separate stones on it. "Milled" fails because that soil survived beneath the ice, which was frozen to the ground, so the ice did not grind the floor. "Incised" fails because the river still wanders across the floor in a shallow bed, so no channel was cut into it.

P32.author: A
P32.explanation: "Blinded" fits: the fog was so thick that lookouts could not see their own ships' sterns, ships had to fire guns to keep their places, and two passed rocks they never saw, so the weather took away the crews' sight. "Becalmed" fails because a steady breeze kept every ship moving at its usual speed. "Beached" fails because the two ships that strayed passed the rocks and reached harbor afloat. "Capsized" fails because the ships reached harbor unharmed.

P33.author: B
P33.explanation: During the fever of 1860 the merchant dosed sick miners with quinine and laudanum from his bottles by weights from a physician's handbook and charged them by the dose, so the store was the camp's "pharmacy": where its medicines were measured out and sold. "Pawnshop" fails because he gave the doses on credit against each man's next cleanup, taking no goods as pledges. "Repository" fails because the safe held his own laudanum and takings, not anything miners deposited. "Parlor" fails because he barred the door at sundown.

P34.author: B
P34.explanation: Soldiers broke open the cases on the first night, stuffed their packs with small valuables, left slashed canvases behind, listed nothing, and later sold the pieces privately, so the army had "ransacked" the collection. "Requisitioned" fails because a requisition is an official taking for an army's use, and here nothing was recorded and the pieces ended up sold by individual soldiers. "Repatriated" fails because the pieces surfaced in shops in the army's home country, not in the neighboring towns they had come from. "Ransomed" fails because the council was asked for nothing and got nothing back.

P35.author: E
P35.explanation: Winter snow piles up on the glacier, and its river runs fullest at the height of summer, when the plain's rain-fed streams dry up and the villages open their ditches, so the glacier holds the winter's water and gives it out in summer: it is the valley's "storeroom." A "thermometer" registers changes in temperature, but the glacier's front has stayed at one ledge through warm decades and cold. A "timepiece" marks the passing hours, but meltwater filtering for days through gravel keeps the river's level nearly the same morning and night. A "signpost" points travelers along a route, but the glacier can be seen only from the last village, where the road ends, so no traveler can steer by it on the way.

P36.author: B
P36.explanation: The herd's size and range stayed the same, but the elk now raised their heads every few seconds, fed a third less, and bolted at a raven's call, so the wolves "rattled" the herd: they made it jumpy without moving or thinning it. "Reduced" fails because the total barely changed. "Redistributed" fails because the meadows held as many elk as ever and the collared cows kept to their old ranges. "Rejuvenated" fails because the few elk the wolves took were mostly calves, so the herd grew older.

P37.author: E
P37.explanation: Every sizable ship had to take a town-licensed pilot to cross, paid a fee the council set, and those fees funded the town, so the bar was the point where the town collected from all traffic: a "tollbooth." A "turnstile" admits traffic one at a time, but pilots took ships over three or four together. A "wharf" is where cargo is handled, but ships unloaded at the town's piers after crossing. A "seawall" shelters a harbor from the sea, but winter swells rolled over the bar and broke against the piers behind it.

P38.author: A
P38.explanation: "Bombarded" fits: alliance warships stood off the harbor, and the enemy's coal depot became a crater with the sheds beside it reduced to rubble, so the warships shelled the port. "Blockaded" fails because freighters of every flag still came and went between attacks, so the harbor was never closed. "Boycotted" fails because the island's wool still sold in the alliance's own markets. "Annexed" fails because the island's flag still flew over the customs house.

P39.author: A
P39.explanation: "Crated" fits: workers took the church down stone by stone, numbering each, so that a college overseas could rebuild it, so the council had it packed up and shipped away. "Condemned" fails because engineers found the walls sound and the tower true. "Bulldozed" fails because the church was not destroyed; it was raised again on the college's lawn, where it still stands. "Commandeered" fails because the college paid the town for the church, so it was sold, not seized for the council's use.

P40.author: D
P40.explanation: Sand settled a few inches a year in the still air behind the walls, families laid new floors and built rooms on top of it, and a well in the main lane now passes through thirty feet of sand and floors to reach the first street, so the sand had "lifted" the village. "Nibbled" fails because the village still fills the same circuit of walls and gave up no part of itself; it rose in place. "Imprisoned" fails because caravans still reach its gate by a ramp. "Lashed" fails because the sand came to rest in still air behind the walls, dropping where the wind slowed, so it was not being driven against the village.
